title: Biochemistry I: Biomolecules and Enzymes (BCH 201)
description: Structure and function of carbohydrates, lipids, amino acids and proteins, nucleic acids, vitamins, and enzymes with their kinetics.

topics.title: Carbohydrates
topics.summary: Monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides, isomerism and glycosidic bonds.

notes.b: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses; fructose is a ketohexose; ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses in nucleic acids. Glucose and galactose are epimers (differ at C-4). In solution, glucose forms α and β ring anomers. Reducing sugars (all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose) reduce Benedict's reagent; sucrose is non-reducing because the anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are joined. Disaccharides: maltose (glucose–glucose, α1→4), lactose (galactose–glucose, β1→4), sucrose (glucose–fructose, α1→β2).
k: Glucose and galactose are C-4 epimers

notes.b: Starch (plant storage) contains amylose (unbranched α1→4) and amylopectin (α1→4 with α1→6 branches). Glycogen (animal storage in liver and muscle) is like amylopectin but more highly branched. Cellulose is β1→4 linked glucose, which humans cannot digest (dietary fibre). Glycosaminoglycans (e.g. hyaluronic acid, heparin, chondroitin sulphate) are repeating disaccharide units found in connective tissue; heparin is an anticoagulant.
k: Glycogen: α1→4 with α1→6 branches, highly branched

topics.title: Lipids and Membranes
topics.summary: Fatty acids, triacylglycerols, phospholipids, cholesterol and lipoproteins.

notes.b: Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group; saturated ones (palmitic C16:0, stearic C18:0) have no double bonds; unsaturated ones (oleic C18:1) have one or more. Linoleic (ω-6) and α-linolenic (ω-3) acids are essential fatty acids that must come from the diet. Triacylglycerols (glycerol + three fatty acids) are the main energy store (9 kcal/g). Phospholipids (e.g. phosphatidylcholine/lecithin) are amphipathic and form membrane bilayers. Sphingolipids include sphingomyelin (myelin) and gangliosides.

Cholesterol is a steroid that stabilises membranes and is the precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D. Lipoproteins transport lipids: chylomicrons (dietary triglyceride from gut, largest, least dense), VLDL (endogenous triglyceride from liver), LDL ('bad' cholesterol, delivers cholesterol to tissues via the LDL receptor; high levels promote atherosclerosis), and HDL ('good' cholesterol, reverse cholesterol transport to the liver). Familial hypercholesterolaemia results from defective LDL receptors.
k: Cholesterol → bile acids, steroids, vitamin D

topics.title: Amino Acids and Proteins
topics.summary: Amino acid classification, peptide bonds, protein structure and denaturation.

notes.b: Twenty standard amino acids share an α-carbon bearing an amino group, a carboxyl group, hydrogen and a variable side chain (R). All except glycine are chiral; proteins contain L-amino acids. At physiological pH they are zwitterions. Classification by R group: non-polar (alanine, valine, leucine), polar uncharged (serine, threonine), acidic (aspartate, glutamate), basic (lysine, arginine, histidine), aromatic (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan). The nine essential amino acids (PVT TIM HLL: phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, leucine, lysine) must come from the diet.

Primary structure is the amino acid sequence joined by peptide bonds (rigid, planar). Secondary structure is local folding stabilised by hydrogen bonds: α-helix and β-pleated sheet (collagen forms a special triple helix rich in glycine and proline). Tertiary structure is the 3-D folding of one chain, stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges (between cysteines). Quaternary structure is the association of subunits (e.g. haemoglobin's four chains). Denaturation (heat, extremes of pH, heavy metals) disrupts higher structure but not peptide bonds.

topics.title: Nucleotides, Nucleic Acids and Vitamins
topics.summary: Nucleotide structure, DNA and RNA, and water- and fat-soluble vitamins with deficiency states.

notes.b: A nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphate. Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine (DNA) and uracil (RNA). DNA is a double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953) with antiparallel strands, A pairing with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three hydrogen bonds); Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C. RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and uracil; types include mRNA, tRNA and rRNA. ATP is the energy currency of the cell.
k: Purines: A, G; pyrimidines: C, T, U

notes.b: Fat-soluble vitamins: A (night blindness, xerophthalmia), D (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults), E (haemolysis, neuropathy), K (bleeding). Water-soluble vitamins: B1 thiamine (beriberi, Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcoholics), B2 riboflavin (angular stomatitis), B3 niacin (pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia), B6 pyridoxine (neuropathy, with isoniazid), B9 folate and B12 cobalamin (megaloblastic anaemia; B12 also causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord), C ascorbic acid (scurvy: bleeding gums, poor wound healing). Many B vitamins are coenzyme precursors: B1 → TPP, B2 → FAD, B3 → NAD+.

topics.title: Enzymes and Enzyme Kinetics
topics.summary: Enzyme classification, coenzymes, Michaelis–Menten kinetics, inhibition and regulation.

notes.b: Enzymes are biological catalysts (mostly proteins) that lower activation energy without altering equilibrium. The six IUBMB classes are oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases. Many require cofactors (metal ions) or coenzymes (organic, often vitamin-derived). The Michaelis–Menten equation: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax — a low Km means high affinity. The Lineweaver–Burk (double reciprocal) plot gives 1/Vmax as the y-intercept and −1/Km as the x-intercept. Activity varies with temperature and pH (pepsin optimum pH ~2; trypsin ~8).
k: Km = [S] at ½Vmax; low Km = high affinity

notes.b: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and bind the active site: Km increases, Vmax unchanged (overcome by more substrate), e.g. statins on HMG-CoA reductase, methotrexate on dihydrofolate reductase. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere: Vmax decreases, Km unchanged. Irreversible inhibitors include organophosphates (acetylcholinesterase) and aspirin (cyclo-oxygenase). Enzymes are regulated by allosteric effectors, covalent modification (phosphorylation), zymogen activation (trypsinogen → trypsin) and induction or repression of synthesis. Isoenzymes (e.g. LDH, CK-MB) help diagnose tissue damage.
k: CK-MB and troponin for myocardial injury
